Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১) Which is a bat shaped bone?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The sphenoid bone is classically described as a bat-shaped bone because of its broad greater wings and smaller lesser wings extending laterally from the central body. It is located at the base of the skull and forms important parts of the cranial floor, orbit, and middle cranial fossa. The sella turcica, which houses the pituitary gland, is located on its body.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sphenoid → bat-shaped

  • Ethmoid → sieve-like

  • Temporal → irregular, paired bone

  • Frontal → forehead and anterior cranial fossa

Exam Pearl:
Bat-shaped bone = Sphenoid.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২) Which group is typical intercostal nerves?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The typical intercostal nerves are T3–T6, so none of the options exactly matches the standard anatomical definition. However, in many exam references, T2–T6 or T2–T8 may be described in relation to intercostal nerve distribution. Among the given options, 2–8 is the best available answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Typical intercostal nerves → T3–T6

  • T1 → mainly contributes to brachial plexus

  • T2 → gives intercostobrachial nerve

  • T7–T11 → thoracoabdominal nerves

  • T12 → subcostal nerve

Exam Pearl:
Strict anatomy: typical intercostal nerves = T3–T6.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩) Which is a membranous organelle?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
A peroxisome is a single-membrane-bound organelle containing oxidative enzymes, including catalase and oxidases. It is involved in fatty acid oxidation and detoxification of harmful substances such as hydrogen peroxide.

The ribosome, centriole, and microtubule are non-membranous structures.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Peroxisome → single membrane

  • Lysosome → single membrane

  • Mitochondria → double membrane

  • Ribosome → non-membranous

  • Centriole → non-membranous

  • Microtubule → non-membranous

Exam Pearl:
Peroxisome = single-membrane-bound organelle.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪) What is the percentage of cholesterol in cell membrane?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Cholesterol constitutes approximately 25% of the lipid content of the cell membrane and is an important component of the phospholipid bilayer. It helps maintain membrane stability and regulate membrane fluidity. Cholesterol prevents excessive membrane fluidity at high temperatures and prevents excessive rigidity at low temperatures.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cholesterol in cell membrane ≈ 25%

  • Maintains membrane stability

  • Regulates membrane fluidity

  • Present between phospholipid molecules

Exam Pearl:
Cell membrane cholesterol ≈ 25% → maintains membrane fluidity and stability.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫) Which is the function of peripheral proteins in cell membrane?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Peripheral membrane proteins are loosely attached to the inner or outer surface of the cell membrane and commonly function as enzymes, structural proteins, or signaling molecules. They do not span the lipid bilayer.

In contrast, integral membrane proteins commonly function as ion channels, carriers, and pumps, because they span or are embedded within the membrane.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Peripheral proteins → enzymes, structural/support functions

  • Integral proteins → channels, carriers, pumps

  • Peripheral proteins → do not span the lipid bilayer.

Exam Pearl:
Peripheral membrane protein → commonly acts as an enzyme.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬) Cell coat is rich in......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The cell coat (glycocalyx) is the carbohydrate-rich layer present on the outer surface of the plasma membrane. It is formed mainly by the carbohydrate portions of glycoproteins, glycolipids, and proteoglycans. It contributes to cell recognition, cell adhesion, receptor interactions, and protection of the cell surface.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cell coat / glycocalyx → carbohydrate-rich

  • Mainly composed of → glycoproteins + glycolipids

  • Functions → cell recognition, adhesion, protection

Exam Pearl:
Cell coat = carbohydrate-rich glycocalyx.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭) Which is not a stage of spermatogenesis?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The classical stages of spermatogenesis are:

  1. Multiplication phase → mitosis of spermatogonia

  2. Growth phase → formation of primary spermatocytes

  3. Maturation phase → meiosis I & II → spermatids

  4. Spermiogenesis → spermatids transform into spermatozoa

“Spermatocytosis” is not a recognized standard stage of spermatogenesis. Therefore, it is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spermatogonia → mitosis

  • Primary spermatocyte → meiosis I

  • Secondary spermatocyte → meiosis II

  • Spermatid → spermiogenesis → spermatozoon

Exam Pearl:
Spermatogenesis = multiplication → growth → maturation → spermiogenesis; “spermatocytosis” is not a standard stage.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮) All are contents of pulmonary ligament except-
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The pulmonary ligament is a double fold of mediastinal pleura below the root of the lung. It contains loose areolar tissue, lymphatics, and bronchial nerves. It also allows movement of the lung root during respiration and provides space for expansion of pulmonary vessels.

An accessory bronchial artery is not a typical content of the pulmonary ligament. Therefore, it is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pulmonary ligament → loose areolar tissue

  • → lymphatics

  • → bronchial nerves

  • Accessory bronchial artery → not a typical content

Exam Pearl:
Pulmonary ligament contains loose tissue, lymphatics and nerves—not an accessory bronchial artery.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯) Which is in relation of medial surface of left lung?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The medial surface of the left lung has several impressions related to mediastinal structures. The most characteristic is the impression of the arch of the aorta, which arches over the root of the left lung and leaves a groove on its medial surface.

The SVC and azygos vein are related mainly to the right lung, while the brachiocephalic trunk is not a characteristic impression on the left lung.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Left lung → arch of aorta impression

  • Left lung → descending thoracic aorta

  • Right lung → SVC and azygos vein

  • Left lung → cardiac impression is deeper than right

Exam Pearl:
Arch of aorta → medial surface of left lung.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১০) Apex of heart formed only by.......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The apex of the heart is formed exclusively by the left ventricle. It is directed downward, forward, and to the left and is located in the left 5th intercostal space near the midclavicular line. The apex is also the site where the apical impulse (cardiac apex beat) is normally palpated.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Apex → left ventricle

  • Anterior surface → mainly right ventricle

  • Base → mainly left atrium + part of right atrium

  • Inferior surface → mainly left and right ventricles

Exam Pearl:
Apex of heart = Left ventricle only.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১১) Which one is the length of thoracic duct?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body and is approximately 30–45 cm long. In standard anatomy MCQs, its length is commonly given as about 38–45 cm, depending on the reference. However, among the given options, 30 cm is often used as the approximate textbook value.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thoracic duct → largest lymphatic vessel

  • Length → approximately 30–45 cm

  • Begins at cisterna chyli

  • Enters thorax through aortic hiatus

  • Terminates at left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins)

Exam Pearl:
Thoracic duct length ≈ 30–45 cm; for this MCQ, choose 30 cm.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১২) Which fascia is replaced by Dartos muscle?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The dartos muscle is a thin layer of smooth muscle in the superficial fascia of the scrotum. In the scrotum, the membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa’s fascia) is replaced by the dartos fascia/muscle. Contraction of dartos produces wrinkling of the scrotal skin and helps regulate testicular temperature.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Scarpa’s fascia → replaced by dartos muscle in scrotum

  • Dartos → smooth muscle

  • Function → scrotal wrinkling + temperature regulation

  • Camper’s fascia → fatty layer of superficial fascia

Exam Pearl:
Dartos muscle replaces Scarpa’s fascia in the scrotum.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৩) Mamillary process found in which vertebra?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The mammillary process is a characteristic feature of lumbar vertebrae. It is a small projection located on the posterior aspect of the superior articular process. It provides attachment for muscles involved in movements and stabilization of the vertebral column, particularly the multifidus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mammillary process → Lumbar vertebra

  • Accessory process → lumbar vertebra

  • Transverse costal facets → thoracic vertebrae

  • Transverse foramen → cervical vertebrae

Exam Pearl:
Mammillary process = Lumbar vertebra.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৪) Inferior vena cava begins at the level of which vertebrae?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The inferior vena cava (IVC) is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the L5 vertebra, just to the right of the midline. It then ascends on the right side of the abdominal aorta and passes through the caval opening of the diaphragm at T8.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IVC begins → L5

  • Common iliac veins unite → L5

  • IVC passes through diaphragm → T8

  • Aorta passes through diaphragm → T12

  • Esophagus → T10

Exam Pearl:
IVC formation = L5; caval opening = T8.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৫) Which one is the largest branch of abdominal aorta?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is the largest unpaired anterior branch of the abdominal aorta. It arises at approximately the L1 vertebral level, just below the celiac trunk, and supplies the midgut, including most of the small intestine and part of the large intestine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Largest branch → Superior mesenteric artery

  • Celiac trunk → foregut

  • SMA → midgut

  • IMA → hindgut

  • SMA originates → L1

Exam Pearl:
Largest branch of abdominal aorta = Superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৬) Cells of epidermis excludes...?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The main cells of the epidermis are keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells, and Langerhans cells. In many exam contexts, the term Langhans cell is considered incorrect here because the correct epidermal immune cell is Langerhans cell. Langhans giant cells are seen in granulomatous inflammation, not as normal epidermal cells. Therefore, Langhans cell is the excluded option.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Keratinocyte → main epidermal cell

  • Melanocyte → pigment cell

  • Merkel cell → tactile cell

  • Langerhans cell → antigen-presenting cell

  • Langhans giant cell → granuloma, not epidermis

Exam Pearl:
Epidermis has keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells, and Langerhans cells — not Langhans cells.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৭) Cristae is present in....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Cristae are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. These folds greatly increase the surface area available for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, thereby facilitating oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cristae → inner mitochondrial membrane

  • Mitochondria → site of oxidative phosphorylation

  • Ribosome → protein synthesis

  • Centriole → microtubule organization

  • Chromosome → genetic material

Exam Pearl:
Cristae = folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৮) Organelles engaged in protein synthesis excludes.......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Ribosomes are the primary sites of protein synthesis. RER has ribosomes attached to its surface and synthesizes proteins destined for secretion, membranes, and lysosomes. Mitochondria also contain their own ribosomes and can synthesize a limited number of mitochondrial proteins. SER, however, lacks ribosomes and is mainly involved in lipid synthesis, steroid synthesis, detoxification, and Ca²⁺ storage. Therefore, SER is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ribosome → protein synthesis

  • RER → protein synthesis

  • Mitochondria → limited protein synthesis

  • SER → lipid synthesis, detoxification, Ca²⁺ storage

Exam Pearl:
SER has no ribosomes → not involved in protein synthesis.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১৯) Which is necessary for synthesis of acrosome in spermatozoa?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The acrosome of the spermatozoon develops from the Golgi complex during spermiogenesis. Golgi-derived vesicles coalesce to form the acrosomal vesicle, which spreads over the anterior part of the sperm nucleus. The acrosome contains hydrolytic enzymes such as acrosin and hyaluronidase that help the sperm penetrate the zona pellucida during fertilization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acrosome → Golgi complex

  • Acrosome develops during spermiogenesis

  • Contains hydrolytic enzymes

  • Helps sperm penetrate zona pellucida

Exam Pearl:
Acrosome formation = Golgi apparatus.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২০) How many ovum is formed from one oogonium in oogenesis?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
From one oogonium, oogenesis ultimately produces one functional ovum. This occurs because meiosis involves unequal cytokinesis, producing one large functional cell and small polar bodies. The unequal division preserves most of the cytoplasm and organelles in the ovum, which is essential for supporting early embryonic development.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 1 oogonium → 1 functional ovum

  • Oogenesis produces polar bodies in addition to the ovum.

  • Spermatogenesis → 1 spermatogonium ultimately produces 4 spermatozoa.

  • Oogenesis → unequal cytoplasmic division.

Exam Pearl:
One oogonium produces one functional ovum.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২১) Diaphragm consists of what type of muscle?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The diaphragm is composed of skeletal muscle, so it is classified as a voluntary (striated) muscle. Although breathing occurs automatically under the control of respiratory centers in the brainstem, the diaphragm can also be voluntarily controlled, such as during breath-holding or forced breathing.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Diaphragm → skeletal/striated muscle

  • Skeletal muscle → voluntary

  • Breathing → normally involuntary/automatic

  • Diaphragm → main muscle of inspiration

Exam Pearl:
Diaphragm is a skeletal (voluntary) muscle, despite its automatic activity during normal breathing.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২২) Microvilli increases how amount of the absorptive area?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Microvilli are finger-like projections of the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells. They markedly increase the absorptive surface area of the small intestine. In standard physiology descriptions, microvilli increase the surface area by approximately 10-fold. Together with plicae circulares and intestinal villi, they produce the enormous absorptive surface of the small intestine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Microvilli → ~10-fold increase

  • Villi → ~10-fold increase

  • Plicae circulares → ~3-fold increase

  • Combined effect → enormous increase in absorptive surface area.

Exam Pearl:
Microvilli increase intestinal absorptive area ≈ 10-fold.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৩) What is vertebrae level of oesophageal opening?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The esophageal hiatus is the opening in the diaphragm through which the esophagus passes. It is located at the level of T10 vertebra. It also transmits the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Esophageal hiatus → T10

  • Caval opening → T8

  • Aortic hiatus → T12

Exam Pearl:
Diaphragmatic openings: T8 = IVC, T10 = Esophagus, T12 = Aorta.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৪) Which is example of fibrocartilage?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Fibrocartilage is a strong type of cartilage that contains abundant type I collagen fibers, making it resistant to both compression and tensile forces. The intervertebral discs are classic examples of fibrocartilage, particularly the annulus fibrosus.

  • Auricle → elastic cartilage

  • Nasal septum → hyaline cartilage

  • Intervertebral disc → fibrocartilage

  • Articular cartilage → hyaline cartilage

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fibrocartilage → intervertebral disc, pubic symphysis, menisci

  • Elastic cartilage → auricle, epiglottis

  • Hyaline cartilage → articular surfaces, trachea, nasal septum

Exam Pearl:
Intervertebral disc = fibrocartilage.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৫) Which is a modified long bone?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The clavicle is classified as a modified long bone. Although it does not have the typical medullary cavity and is horizontally oriented, it has a shaft and two ends, resembling a long bone. It is also the first bone to begin ossification during embryonic development and ossifies mainly by intramembranous ossification.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Clavicle → modified long bone

  • Fibula → typical long bone

  • Metacarpals → long bones

  • Phalanges → long bones

  • Clavicle → first bone to ossify

Exam Pearl:
Clavicle = modified long bone.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৬) Which is located at Howship's lacunae?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Howship’s lacunae are shallow depressions on the surface of bone formed by bone resorption. They contain osteoclasts, the multinucleated cells responsible for bone resorption.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Howship’s lacunae → Osteoclast

  • Osteoclast → bone resorption

  • Osteoblast → bone formation

  • Osteocyte → lies in lacunae within bone

  • Osteoprogenitor cell → precursor of osteoblasts

Exam Pearl:
Howship’s lacuna = Osteoclast.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৭) Which is example of aberrant epiphysis?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
An aberrant (atypical) epiphysis is an epiphysis that develops at a site other than the usual end of a long bone. The coracoid process of the scapula is a classic example of an aberrant epiphysis, developing from a separate ossification center and later fusing with the scapula.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aberrant epiphysis → coracoid process of scapula

  • Head of humerus → typical epiphysis

  • Trochanters of femur → traction/apophyseal epiphyses

  • 1st metacarpal → atypical long bone development

Exam Pearl:
Coracoid process = classic example of aberrant epiphysis.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৮) Gastrulation occurs in.....week of development?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Gastrulation occurs during the 3rd week of embryonic development. It transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar embryonic disc consisting of:

  • Ectoderm

  • Mesoderm

  • Endoderm

The key event is the formation of the primitive streak, through which cells migrate to form the intraembryonic mesoderm and definitive endoderm.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Week 1 → cleavage, morula, blastocyst

  • Week 2 → implantation + bilaminar disc

  • Week 3 → gastrulation + trilaminar disc

  • Week 4 → folding of embryo

Exam Pearl:
Gastrulation = 3rd week = trilaminar germ disc formation.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ২৯) What is the type of sternoclavicular joint?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The sternoclavicular (SC) joint is a synovial saddle joint. It is formed between the medial end of the clavicle, the clavicular notch of the manubrium, and the first costal cartilage. An articular disc divides the joint cavity and improves its stability.

The SC joint permits elevation/depression, protraction/retraction, and some rotation of the clavicle, allowing a wide range of shoulder movements.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sternoclavicular joint → Saddle

  • Acromioclavicular joint → Plane

  • Shoulder joint → Ball-and-socket

  • Elbow → Hinge

  • Atlantoaxial → Pivot

Exam Pearl:
SC joint = synovial saddle joint.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩০) Which is not a criteria of skeletal muscle?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Skeletal muscle is characterized by multiple peripheral nuclei, prominent cross-striations, and voluntary control. Skeletal muscle fibers are generally long, cylindrical, and unbranched. Therefore, branching is not a characteristic of skeletal muscle.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Skeletal muscle → multiple peripheral nuclei

  • → cross-striated

  • → voluntary

  • → long, cylindrical, unbranched

  • Cardiac muscle → branching + single central nucleus + intercalated discs

Exam Pearl:
Branching is a feature of cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩১) Visceral musculature develops from....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.option3: somatopleuric layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.option4: splanchnopleuric layer of lateral plate mesoderm
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The visceral musculature (smooth muscle) of the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts develops mainly from the splanchnopleuric layer of lateral plate mesoderm. This layer is formed by the association of splanchnic mesoderm with endoderm and gives rise to much of the connective tissue and smooth muscle of the visceral organs.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Visceral smooth muscle → splanchnopleuric mesoderm

  • Skeletal muscle → paraxial mesoderm (somites)

  • Urogenital system → intermediate mesoderm

  • Somatopleuric mesoderm → body wall connective tissues and limb structures

Exam Pearl:
Visceral musculature = splanchnopleuric lateral plate mesoderm.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩২) The fetal part of placenta develops from....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The fetal part of the placenta develops from the chorion frondosum, which consists of the chorionic plate and its branching chorionic villi. The maternal part develops from the decidua basalis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fetal part → Chorion frondosum

  • Maternal part → Decidua basalis

  • Chorion frondosum → villous chorion

  • Chorion laeve → smooth, non-villous chorion

Exam Pearl:
Placenta = fetal part (chorion frondosum) + maternal part (decidua basalis).

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৩) Ectrodactyly means?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Ectrodactyly is a congenital limb anomaly characterized by absence or severe deficiency of one or more digits, often producing a characteristic split-hand or split-foot appearance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ectrodactyly → absence/deficiency of digits

  • Polydactyly → extra digits

  • Brachydactyly → short digits

  • Syndactyly → fusion of digits

Exam Pearl:
Ectrodactyly = missing/deficient digits ("split hand/foot").

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৪) Gastric glands lies in which layer?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The gastric glands are located in the lamina propria of the mucosa. They extend from the gastric pits downward through the mucosa and contain different cell types, including parietal cells, chief cells, mucous cells, and enteroendocrine cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric glands → lamina propria

  • Gastric pits → mucosa

  • Meissner’s plexus → submucosa

  • Auerbach’s plexus → muscularis propria

Exam Pearl:
Gastric glands lie in the lamina propria.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৫) Which vein drain into portal system?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The superior rectal vein drains into the inferior mesenteric vein, which ultimately joins the portal venous system. In contrast, the middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac vein → IVC, forming part of the systemic circulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Superior rectal vein → portal system

  • Middle rectal vein → systemic circulation

  • Inferior rectal vein → systemic circulation

  • Rectal venous plexus → site of portosystemic anastomosis

Exam Pearl:
Superior rectal vein = portal drainage; middle & i

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৬) Which one is the most common position of appendix?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The retrocecal position is the most common position of the vermiform appendix, accounting for approximately 60–65% of cases. In this position, the appendix lies behind the cecum and may extend upward toward the ascending colon.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common → Retrocecal

  • Pelvic → second most common

  • Subcecal → less common

  • Preileal/postileal → uncommon

Exam Pearl:
Most common position of appendix = Retrocecal.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৭) Which one is the main support of liver?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The main support of the liver is provided by its surrounding viscera, particularly the abdominal organs and diaphragm. Although the liver has several peritoneal ligaments—such as the falciform, coronary, and triangular ligaments—these primarily help maintain its position rather than providing its main mechanical support.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Main support of liver → surrounding viscera

  • Ligaments → help maintain position

  • Diaphragm → important superior support

  • Hepatic veins → drainage, not support

Exam Pearl:
Liver is mainly supported by surrounding viscera and the diaphragm.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৮) Which gland is largest in our body?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The liver is the largest gland in the human body, weighing approximately 1.2–1.5 kg in an adult. It is a mixed gland because it has both exocrine and endocrine functions. It produces bile as an exocrine secretion and releases various substances, such as plasma proteins, into the blood.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Largest gland → Liver

  • Largest endocrine gland → Thyroid

  • Largest exocrine gland → Liver

  • Largest organ → Skin

Exam Pearl:
Largest gland = Liver; largest organ = Skin.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৩৯) Which one is not a histological layer of gallbladder?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The gallbladder does not have a distinct submucosa. Its wall consists mainly of:

  • Mucosa → simple columnar epithelium with lamina propria

  • Fibromuscular layer → smooth muscle with connective tissue

  • Perimuscular connective tissue

  • Serosa → on the free peritoneal surface

Therefore, submucosa is not a histological layer of the gallbladder.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gallbladder → no muscularis mucosa

  • Gallbladder → no submucosa

  • Mucosa → simple columnar epithelium

  • Fibromuscular layer → smooth muscle

Exam Pearl:
Gallbladder lacks a submucosal layer.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪০) Spleen develops from........?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The spleen develops from mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium during the 5th week of embryonic development. It is therefore mesodermal in origin. As the stomach rotates, the dorsal mesogastrium elongates and contributes to the formation of the greater omentum, gastrosplenic ligament, and splenorenal ligament.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spleen → dorsal mesogastrium

  • Embryological origin → mesoderm

  • Liver → endoderm-derived hepatic diverticulum

  • Ventral mesogastrium → lesser omentum + falciform ligament

Exam Pearl:
Spleen develops from mesenchyme of the dorsal mesogastrium.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪১) All are the site of portacaval anastomosis except......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Portocaval (portosystemic) anastomoses occur where tributaries of the portal venous system communicate with tributaries of the systemic venous system.

Common sites include:

  • Esophagus → left gastric ↔ azygos veins

  • Rectum → superior rectal ↔ middle/inferior rectal veins

  • Stomach → gastric veins ↔ systemic venous channels

The liver is not a site of portocaval anastomosis; portal blood normally enters the liver through the portal vein and leaves through the hepatic veins.

Exam Pearl:
Portocaval anastomosis sites: esophagus, stomach, rectum, umbilicus, retroperitoneum — not liver.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪২) Which one is commonest anomaly of kidney?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The horseshoe kidney is the commonest renal fusion anomaly and is the best answer among the given options. It results from fusion of the lower poles of the two kidneys, usually during early embryonic development. The fused kidney remains lower than normal because its ascent is prevented by the inferior mesenteric artery.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Horseshoe kidney → commonest fusion anomaly

  • Usually fusion of lower poles

  • Ascent prevented by inferior mesenteric artery

  • Usually lies at a lower level than normal kidneys

Exam Pearl:
Commonest renal fusion anomaly = Horseshoe kidney.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৩) Which one is most constricted part of male urethra?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The external urethral orifice (external meatus) is the narrowest/constricted part of the male urethra. It is located at the tip of the glans penis and is surrounded by the fossa navicularis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Narrowest part → external urethral meatus

  • Membranous urethra → least distensible part

  • Prostatic urethra → widest part

  • Penile/spongy urethra → relatively wide and distensible

Exam Pearl:
Narrowest part of male urethra = external urethral orifice.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৪) (সঠিক উত্তর গ ও ঘ। তাই প্রশ্নটি বাতিল করা হয়েছে।) Fallopian tube develops from........?
৪৫) Which is a merocrine gland?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Merocrine glands release their secretions by exocytosis, without loss of cytoplasm. Most digestive glands (e.g., pancreatic and salivary glands) are merocrine.

  • Sebaceous gland → holocrine

  • Tarsal (Meibomian) gland → holocrine

  • Mammary gland → mainly apocrine for lipid secretion and merocrine for protein secretion

  • Digestive glands → merocrine

Exam Pearl:
Digestive glands are classic examples of merocrine glands.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৬) Which one is compound tubuloacinar gland?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The submandibular gland is a compound tubuloacinar (tubuloalveolar) gland. It contains both mucous tubules and serous acini, making it a mixed gland, with predominantly serous secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Parotid → compound acinar (serous)

  • Submandibular → compound tubuloacinar (mixed, mainly serous)

  • Sublingual → compound tubuloacinar (mixed, mainly mucous)

  • Sweat gland → simple coiled tubular

Exam Pearl:
Submandibular gland = compound tubuloacinar, mixed gland.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৭) Which is unicellular gland?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Goblet cells are unicellular exocrine glands. They are specialized epithelial cells that secrete mucin, which forms mucus. They are commonly found among the epithelial cells of the intestine and respiratory tract.

The sweat, salivary, and palatine glands are multicellular exocrine glands.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Goblet cell → unicellular gland

  • Secretion → mucin/mucus

  • Sweat gland → multicellular tubular gland

  • Salivary gland → multicellular compound gland

Exam Pearl:
Goblet cell = classic example of a unicellular exocrine gland.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৮) Which is dense irregular connective tissue?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The dermis is mainly composed of dense irregular connective tissue, particularly its reticular layer. The collagen fibers are arranged in multiple directions, providing strength against stresses from different directions.

  • Tendon → dense regular connective tissue

  • Ligament → dense regular connective tissue

  • Dermis → dense irregular connective tissue

  • Fascia → mainly connective tissue with variable composition

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dense regular → tendon, ligament

  • Dense irregular → dermis, organ capsules

  • Dense irregular fibers → arranged in multiple directions

Exam Pearl:
Dermis = dense irregular connective tissue.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৪৯) Which is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy in fallopian tube?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The ampulla is the most common site of ectopic pregnancy in the fallopian tube, accounting for approximately 70% of tubal ectopic pregnancies. The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the uterine tube and is also the usual site of fertilization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ampulla → most common site of tubal ectopic pregnancy

  • Isthmus → narrower medial part

  • Fimbriae → funnel-shaped lateral end

  • Interstitial part → passes through uterine wall

Exam Pearl:
Tubal ectopic pregnancy → most commonly in the ampulla.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫০) Which is a wandering cell?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Mast cells are classically considered wandering cells of connective tissue. They are derived from hematopoietic precursors and can migrate into connective tissues, where they participate in inflammatory and allergic reactions by releasing histamine, heparin, and other mediators.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Wandering cells → mast cells, macrophages, plasma cells, lymphocytes

  • Fixed cells → fibroblasts, adipocytes, reticular cells

  • Mast cell → histamine + heparin

  • Plasma cell → antibody production

Exam Pearl:
Mast cell = classic wandering cell of connective tissue.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫১) Which helps in wound healing?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Fibroblasts play a major role in wound healing by producing collagen, extracellular matrix, and other connective tissue components. During the proliferative phase, fibroblasts migrate into the wound and form granulation tissue, contributing to tissue repair and scar formation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fibroblast → collagen synthesis + wound healing

  • Macrophage → phagocytosis + inflammatory regulation

  • Chondroblast → cartilage formation

  • Adipocyte → fat storage

Exam Pearl:
Fibroblast = key cell for collagen deposition and wound healing.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫২) Mesangial cells are present in......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Mesangial cells are specialized cells located within the renal glomerulus. They provide structural support to glomerular capillaries, have contractile properties, and can perform phagocytic functions. They also help regulate the glomerular filtration surface area.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mesangial cells → kidney

  • Location → glomerulus

  • Functions → structural support, contraction, phagocytosis

  • Also involved in regulation of GFR

Exam Pearl:
Mesangial cells = glomerulus of the kidney.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৩) Type-2 collagen fibre is present in.....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Type II collagen is the principal collagen found in cartilage, especially hyaline cartilage and elastic cartilage. It provides tensile strength and helps cartilage resist deformation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Type I → skin, tendon, bone, dentin

  • Type II → cartilage

  • Type III → reticular fibers

  • Type IV → basement membrane

Exam Pearl:
Type II collagen = cartilage.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৪) Which is not a part of decidua?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The decidua is the endometrium of the uterus during pregnancy and is divided into three main parts:

  • Decidua basalis → beneath the implanted embryo; contributes to the maternal part of placenta.

  • Decidua capsularis → covers the implanted embryo.

  • Decidua parietalis (vera) → remaining uterine lining away from implantation.

Decidua semilunaris is not a recognized part of the decidua.

Exam Pearl:
Decidua = basalis + capsularis + parietalis (vera).

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৫) Which one is the largest nerve of lumbar plexus?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The femoral nerve (L2–L4) is the largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It supplies the anterior compartment of the thigh, including the quadriceps, and provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg through the saphenous nerve.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Largest nerve of lumbar plexus → Femoral nerve

  • Roots → L2–L4

  • Motor → quadriceps and sartorius

  • Sensory → anterior thigh + medial leg/foot via saphenous nerve

  • Sciatic nerve → largest nerve of the body, not lumbar plexus.

Exam Pearl:
Femoral nerve = largest branch of lumbar plexus.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৬) Foot drop occur due to injury of which nerve?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Foot drop occurs mainly due to paralysis of the dorsiflexors of the foot, particularly tibialis anterior. These muscles are supplied by the deep peroneal (deep fibular) nerve, derived from the common peroneal nerve.

Injury causes inability to dorsiflex the ankle, resulting in high-stepping gait.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Deep peroneal nerve → dorsiflexion

  • Tibialis anterior → main dorsiflexor

  • Deep peroneal nerve injury → foot drop

  • Superficial peroneal nerve → mainly eversion

Exam Pearl:
Foot drop = common peroneal/deep peroneal nerve injury; in this MCQ → deep peroneal nerve.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৭) Which is called the beauty bone?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The clavicle (collar bone) is popularly called the “beauty bone” because it is a prominent, visible bone beneath the skin that contributes to the contour of the neck and shoulder.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Beauty bone → Clavicle

  • Clavicle → connects upper limb to axial skeleton

  • Acts as a strut keeping the upper limb away from the thorax

  • It is the first bone to ossify during development.

Exam Pearl:
Beauty bone = Clavicle.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৮) Winging of scapula results from injury to which nerve?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) supplies the serratus anterior muscle. Injury causes paralysis of serratus anterior, resulting in medial winging of the scapula, especially when the patient pushes against a wall.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Long thoracic nerve → Serratus anterior

  • Injury → winging of scapula

  • Roots → C5, C6, C7

  • Clinical test → wall-pushing test

Exam Pearl:
Winging of scapula = long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior paralysis.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৫৯) Rotator cuff is formed by all except.....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The rotator cuff is formed by four muscles, remembered as SITS:

  • Supraspinatus

  • Infraspinatus

  • Teres minor

  • Subscapularis

Teres major is not a member of the rotator cuff. It is a powerful medial rotator and adductor of the arm.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • SITS → Rotator cuff

  • Supraspinatus → initiates abduction

  • Infraspinatus → lateral rotation

  • Teres minor → lateral rotation

  • Subscapularis → medial rotation

  • Teres major → NOT rotator cuff

Exam Pearl:
Rotator cuff = SITS; teres major is the exception.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬০) Which is not a branch of posterior cord of brachial plexus?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The posterior cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to:

  • Upper subscapular nerve

  • Thoracodorsal nerve

  • Lower subscapular nerve

  • Axillary nerve

  • Radial nerve

The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk, not the posterior cord.

Exam Pearl:
Suprascapular nerve → Upper trunk; Upper & lower subscapular + axillary → Posterior cord.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬১) Which one is 1st order neuron of visual pathway?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
In the visual pathway, the bipolar cell is considered the 1st-order neuron. Photoreceptors (rods and cones) receive light and synapse with bipolar cells. Bipolar cells then synapse with ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve (CN II).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 1st-order neuron → Bipolar cell

  • 2nd-order neuron → Ganglion cell

  • Rods/cones → Photoreceptors, not neurons of the classic 3-neuron pathway

  • Ganglion cell axons → Optic nerve → optic chiasma → optic tract

Exam Pearl:
Visual pathway: Bipolar → Ganglion → Lateral geniculate body.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬২) Which one is devoid of taste bud?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the tongue and are devoid of taste buds. They primarily provide mechanical functions, helping grip and manipulate food.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Vallate → taste buds present

  • Fungiform → taste buds present

  • Foliate → taste buds present

  • Filiform → NO taste buds

Exam Pearl:
Filiform papillae = no taste buds; purely mechanical.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৩)  Which one is a part of bony labyrinth?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp: Here, utricle, saccule, and organ of Corti are parts of the membranous labyrinth/inner ear structures, whereas the cochlea is a component of the bony labyrinth.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৪) Thyroid gland develops from which germ layer?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The thyroid gland develops mainly from an endodermal epithelial diverticulum arising from the floor of the primitive pharynx, at the foramen cecum. The thyroid follicular cells are therefore endoderm-derived.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thyroid follicular cells → Endoderm

  • Origin → floor of primitive pharynx

  • Medullary (C) cells → derived from neural crest cells via the ultimobranchial body

Exam Pearl:
Thyroid gland = endodermal origin.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৫) Which is not an adherens junction?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Zonula occludens is a tight junction, not an anchoring/adherens junction. It mainly prevents paracellular movement between epithelial cells.

  • Zonula adherens → adherens junction

  • Desmosome → anchoring junction between cells

  • Hemidesmosome → anchoring junction between cell and basement membrane

  • Zonula occludens → tight junction

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tight junction → Zonula occludens

  • Cell–cell anchoring → Zonula adherens + desmosome

  • Cell–basement membrane anchoring → Hemidesmosome

Exam Pearl:
Zonula occludens = tight junction, not adherens junction.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৬) Which one is present in spermatozoa?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
A spermatozoon possesses a flagellum, which forms its long tail and provides motility. The flagellum contains the characteristic 9+2 arrangement of microtubules in its axoneme.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spermatozoa → Flagellum

  • Flagellum → motility

  • Axoneme → 9+2 microtubule arrangement

  • Microvilli → absorption

  • Stereocilia → epididymis, sensory structures

  • Cilia → respiratory tract, uterine tube

Exam Pearl:
Sperm tail = flagellum → motility.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৭) Which is not a characteristic of epithelial tissue?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Epithelial tissue can develop from all three germ layers—ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Therefore, saying epithelial tissue is specifically originated from ectoderm is incorrect.

Other features are characteristic:

  • Maximum cellularity + minimum ECM → characteristic

  • Avascular → no blood vessels within epithelium

  • Nerve supply present → generally innervated

Exam Pearl:
Epithelium can arise from all 3 germ layers, not only ectoderm.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৮) What is the location of pseudostratified non ciliated epithelium?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Pseudostratified non-ciliated columnar epithelium is found in parts of the male urethra, particularly the membranous/spongy portions.

  • Trachea → pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium

  • Uterine tube → simple ciliated columnar epithelium

  • Male urethra → pseudostratified non-ciliated columnar epithelium

  • Epidermis → keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

Exam Pearl:
Pseudostratified non-ciliated epithelium → male urethra.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৬৯) The gestational period is divided into how many stages?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The gestational period is divided into three trimesters:

  1. 1st trimester → 1–12 weeks

  2. 2nd trimester → 13–27 weeks

  3. 3rd trimester → 28–40 weeks

Exam Pearl:
Gestational period = 3 trimesters.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭০) Which is not true about vein?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Veins generally have large lumens, thin walls, and slower blood flow compared with arteries. Many veins, especially in the limbs, contain valves that prevent backflow of blood and assist venous return.

Exam Pearl:
Veins → large lumen + thin wall + slow flow + valves (often present).

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭১) What is the lining epithelium of conjunctiva?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The conjunctiva is lined mainly by stratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells. It is a non-keratinized epithelium and contributes to the mucous layer of the tear film.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Conjunctiva → stratified columnar epithelium

  • Contains goblet cells

  • Goblet cells → secrete mucin

  • Helps maintain the tear film

Exam Pearl:
Conjunctiva = stratified columnar epithelium + goblet cells.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭২) What type of epithelium helps in protection, distensibility & prevention of reabsorption?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Transitional epithelium (urothelium) is specialized for protection and distensibility. It lines the urinary bladder, ureters, and renal pelvis. Its superficial umbrella cells allow the epithelium to stretch as urine volume increases and form a tight barrier that prevents back-diffusion/reabsorption of urine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Transitional epithelium → urinary tract

  • Functions → protection + distensibility + prevents reabsorption

  • Classic site → urinary bladder

Exam Pearl:
Protection + distensibility + prevention of urine reabsorption = transitional epithelium.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৩) Goblet cells are numerous in.......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Goblet cells are mucus-secreting epithelial cells that produce mucin, which lubricates and protects the intestinal mucosa. Their number progressively increases from the duodenum to the colon. The large intestine (colon) contains the highest density of goblet cells because its primary functions include water absorption and formation of feces, requiring abundant mucus to facilitate fecal passage and protect the mucosa from mechanical injury. The small intestine contains goblet cells but in lower numbers. The stomach predominantly contains surface mucous cells rather than goblet cells, while the gallbladder normally lacks goblet cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Goblet cells secrete mucin, which forms protective mucus.

  • Goblet cell density increases from duodenum → jejunum → ileum → colon.

  • Large intestine has the maximum number of goblet cells.

  • Stomach contains surface mucous cells, not true goblet cells.

  • Gallbladder normally has simple columnar absorptive epithelium without goblet cells.

Exam Pearl: The colon has the greatest concentration of goblet cells in the gastrointestinal tract because of its need for abundant mucus to lubricate feces and protect the mucosa.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৪) Morula consists of....... cells?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The morula is a solid ball of blastomeres formed after successive cleavage divisions of the zygote, typically about 3–4 days after fertilization. It is classically composed of 16 cells, although early and late morulae may contain approximately 16–32 cells. In embryology and medical entrance examinations, the accepted answer is 16 cells. Following the morula stage, fluid enters the embryo to form the blastocyst, which contains an inner cell mass (embryoblast) and an outer cell mass (trophoblast).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 2-cell stage: ~30 hours after fertilization.

  • 8-cell stage: Compaction begins.

  • Morula: 16 cells, forms around day 3–4.

  • Blastocyst: Forms around day 5.

  • Implantation: Begins around day 6–7.

Exam Pearl: Morula = 16-cell solid ball of blastomeres; Blastocyst = fluid-filled stage with embryoblast and trophoblast.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৫) Filum terminale is a continuation of which layer of meninges?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The filum terminale is a slender fibrous extension of the pia mater that anchors the spinal cord inferiorly. It begins at the conus medullaris (approximately the L1–L2 vertebral level in adults) as the filum terminale internum, which extends to the end of the dural sac at the S2 level. Beyond this point, it acquires a dural covering to form the filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament), which attaches to the coccyx. Although the external part is surrounded by dura, the filum terminale itself is a continuation of the pia mater, making pia the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Filum terminale is a continuation of the pia mater.

  • Conus medullaris: Ends at L1–L2 in adults.

  • Filum terminale internum: Conus medullaris to S2 (within the dural sac).

  • Filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament): S2 to coccyx, enclosed by dura.

  • Cauda equina consists of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal nerve roots below the conus medullaris.

Exam Pearl: The filum terminale originates from the pia mater; its external portion is covered by dura but is not derived from it.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৬) Which type of neuron is absent in adult human?
৭৭) Which one is the content of white matter?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
xplanation: White matter of the central nervous system consists predominantly of myelinated nerve fibers (axons), which give it its characteristic white appearance due to the lipid-rich myelin sheath. These fibers are organized into ascending, descending, and commissural tracts that transmit signals between different regions of the brain and spinal cord. In contrast, gray matter primarily contains neuronal cell bodies (soma), dendrites, synapses, and unmyelinated axons. Although glial cells, including astrocytes, are present in white matter, they are not its principal structural component. Therefore, fibers is the single best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • White matter: Predominantly myelinated axons (nerve fibers).

  • Gray matter: Contains neuronal cell bodies (soma), dendrites, and synapses.

  • Myelin in the CNS is produced by oligodendrocytes.

  • Ascending and descending tracts are located in white matter.

  • Astrocytes are present in both gray and white matter but do not constitute the main content.

Exam Pearl: White matter = myelinated nerve fibers; Gray matter = neuronal cell bodies (soma).

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৮) Which one is most dilated part of spinal cord?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The spinal cord has two enlargements: the cervical enlargement and the lumbosacral enlargement. The cervical enlargement (C4–T1 spinal cord segments) is the largest and most dilated because it contains the increased number of neurons required to innervate the upper limbs through the brachial plexus. The lumbosacral enlargement (L2–S3 segments) supplies the lower limbs but is smaller than the cervical enlargement. The thoracic and sacral regions do not show comparable enlargement.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cervical enlargement: C4–T1 spinal cord segments; supplies the upper limb.

  • Lumbosacral enlargement: L2–S3 spinal cord segments; supplies the lower limb.

  • Cervical enlargement is larger than the lumbosacral enlargement.

  • Brachial plexus: Formed by C5–T1 ventral rami.

  • Lumbar is the correct spelling (not "lumber").

Exam Pearl: The cervical enlargement is the largest enlargement of the spinal cord because it contains the neurons supplying the upper limbs via the brachial plexus.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৭৯) Which one carry vibration sense?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Vibration sense, along with fine touch, conscious proprioception, and discriminative touch, is transmitted through the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway. The fasciculus gracilis (Tract of Goll) carries these sensations from the lower limb and lower trunk (below T6), while the fasciculus cuneatus (Tract of Burdach) carries them from the upper limb and upper trunk (above T6). In contrast, the tectospinal, vestibulospinal, and olivospinal tracts are descending motor pathways and do not transmit sensory modalities such as vibration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • DCML pathway carries vibration, fine touch, and conscious proprioception.

  • Fasciculus gracilis (Tract of Goll): Lower limb and lower trunk (below T6).

  • Fasciculus cuneatus (Tract of Burdach): Upper limb and upper trunk (above T6).

  • Fibers decussate in the medulla as internal arcuate fibers.

  • Spinothalamic tract carries pain, temperature, and crude touch.

Exam Pearl: Vibration sense travels in the dorsal columns—Tract of Goll (gracilis) for the lower body and Tract of Burdach (cuneatus) for the upper body.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮০) What are the number of spinal nerve?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The human body has 31 pairs of spinal nerves, each formed by the union of a dorsal (sensory) root and a ventral (motor) root. These nerves emerge from the spinal cord through the intervertebral foramina and provide sensory, motor, and autonomic innervation to the trunk and limbs. The 31 pairs are distributed as 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal spinal nerves. Although there are only 7 cervical vertebrae, there are 8 cervical spinal nerves because the first cervical nerve exits above the atlas (C1), and C8 exits between the C7 and T1 vertebrae.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Total spinal nerves: 31 pairs.

  • Distribution: 8 Cervical, 12 Thoracic, 5 Lumbar, 5 Sacral, 1 Coccygeal (8-12-5-5-1).

  • Each spinal nerve is a mixed nerve (sensory + motor fibers).

  • C1–C7 spinal nerves exit above their corresponding vertebrae.

  • C8 exits between C7 and T1; thoracic and lower spinal nerves exit below their corresponding vertebrae.

Exam Pearl: Remember the formula: 8C + 12T + 5L + 5S + 1Co = 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮১) Which acts as intracellular scavenger?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing numerous acid hydrolases that digest damaged organelles, microorganisms, and intracellular debris. They act as the cell's intracellular scavenger by carrying out heterophagy (digestion of engulfed material) and autophagy (degradation of worn-out organelles). This recycling function is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis. In contrast, ribosomes synthesize proteins, the endoplasmic reticulum is involved in protein and lipid synthesis, and the Golgi complex modifies, packages, and sorts proteins for secretion or intracellular use.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases active at an acidic pH.

  • Functions: Autophagy, heterophagy, and intracellular digestion.

  • Known as the intracellular scavenger or the cell's digestive system.

  • Golgi apparatus forms primary lysosomes by packaging lysosomal enzymes.

  • Lysosomal enzyme deficiencies cause lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick).

Exam Pearl: Lysosomes are the intracellular scavengers because they digest and recycle damaged organelles and cellular waste through autophagy and intracellular digestion.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮২) Which one is essential for cell division?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Centrioles are cylindrical organelles that play a crucial role in cell division by organizing the mitotic spindle through the centrosome. The spindle fibers attach to chromosomes and ensure their accurate separation into daughter cells during mitosis and meiosis. Although the nucleus and chromosomes are indispensable because they contain the genetic material, the standard exam answer to the question asking which organelle is essential for cell division is centriole, owing to its role in spindle formation. Higher plant cells lack centrioles but can still divide using alternative microtubule-organizing centers; however, in human cells, centrioles are classically associated with cell division.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Centrioles are located in the centrosome near the nucleus.

  • They organize the mitotic spindle during mitosis and meiosis.

  • Each centriole is composed of 9 triplets of microtubules (9 × 3 arrangement).

  • Chromosomes carry genetic material; centrioles facilitate chromosome segregation.

  • Mature centrioles also give rise to basal bodies of cilia and flagella.

Exam Pearl: The classic histology answer is: Centrioles are essential for spindle formation during cell division.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৩) Which one participates in muscular contraction?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Microfilaments are cytoskeletal structures composed of actin and play a central role in muscle contraction. During contraction, actin microfilaments interact with myosin thick filaments through the sliding filament mechanism, resulting in shortening of the sarcomere. Although myosin is the motor protein that generates force, it is not a cytoskeletal filament. Since the question asks which structure participates in muscular contraction, the best answer is microfilament. Microtubules are involved in intracellular transport and mitotic spindle formation, while intermediate filaments provide mechanical strength and structural support.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Microfilaments are composed of actin (diameter ≈ 7 nm).

  • Myosin forms the thick filament of skeletal muscle.

  • Microtubules (25 nm) are made of tubulin and form the mitotic spindle, cilia, and flagella.

  • Intermediate filaments provide tensile strength and structural support.

  • Calcium binds troponin C, allowing actin–myosin interaction.

Exam Pearl: Muscle contraction depends on the interaction between actin (microfilament) and myosin; if the question asks for a cytoskeletal element, the correct answer is microfilament.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৪) Which cell has no nucleus?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Mature red blood cells (RBCs) in mammals are anucleate, meaning they lack a nucleus. During erythropoiesis in the bone marrow, the nucleus is extruded at the orthochromatic erythroblast stage. Loss of the nucleus creates more intracellular space for hemoglobin, increases flexibility, and facilitates passage through narrow capillaries. In contrast, muscle cells (skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated), chondrocytes (cartilage cells), and neurons all contain nuclei. Therefore, the mature RBC is the only correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mature mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus and mitochondria.

  • Reticulocytes are immature RBCs that contain residual ribosomal RNA but no nucleus.

  • Absence of mitochondria ensures RBCs do not consume the oxygen they transport.

  • Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated; cardiac and smooth muscle cells usually have a single nucleus.

  • Neurons are generally uninucleate.

Exam Pearl: Mature mammalian RBCs are anucleate, maximizing hemoglobin content and deformability for efficient oxygen transport.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৫) Graafian follicle contains.....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The Graafian (mature) follicle contains a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II of meiosis. Just before ovulation, the primary oocyte completes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte is then ovulated and remains arrested in metaphase II until fertilization. Only upon fertilization does it complete meiosis II to become a mature ovum. Therefore, a Graafian follicle does not contain a mature ovum. The term tertiary oocyte is not used in normal human embryology.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary oocyte: Arrested in prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

  • Graafian follicle: Contains a secondary oocyte.

  • Secondary oocyte: Arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.

  • Meiosis II is completed only after fertilization.

  • Tertiary oocyte is not a recognized stage in human oogenesis.

Exam Pearl: A mature (Graafian) follicle contains a secondary oocyte—not a mature ovum. The ovum forms only after fertilization completes meiosis II.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৬) Which is not true about DNA?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: In eukaryotic cells, DNA is tightly associated with histone proteins, forming nucleosomes, the fundamental units of chromatin. Therefore, the statement "histone absent" is not true for eukaryotic DNA. The other options are correct: DNA is typically a double-stranded molecule, it follows Chargaff's rule (A = T and G = C in double-stranded DNA), and mutations can occur due to replication errors or exposure to mutagens. Although most bacteria lack true histones (they possess histone-like proteins), in standard MBBS and postgraduate examinations, the question refers to human/eukaryotic DNA.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) form the nucleosome core; H1 is the linker histone.

  • DNA is usually double-stranded and antiparallel.

  • Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C in double-stranded DNA.

  • Mutations may be spontaneous or induced by physical, chemical, or biological agents.

  • Mitochondrial DNA is circular but lacks histones.

Exam Pearl: Human (eukaryotic) DNA is associated with histones; therefore, "histone absent" is the false statement.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৭) Mitosis occurs in which phase of cell cycle?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Mitosis occurs during the M (mitotic) phase of the cell cycle. The cell cycle consists of Interphase (G1, S, and G2 phases) followed by the M phase. During G1, the cell grows and synthesizes proteins. In the S phase, DNA replication occurs. During G2, the cell prepares for mitosis by synthesizing proteins and checking for DNA damage. The M phase includes mitosis (prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase) followed by cytokinesis, resulting in two genetically identical daughter cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • G1 phase: Cell growth and protein synthesis.

  • S phase: DNA replication.

  • G2 phase: Preparation for mitosis; DNA damage checkpoint.

  • M phase: Mitosis + cytokinesis.

  • Cell cycle checkpoints: G1/S, G2/M, and metaphase (spindle) checkpoint.

Exam Pearl: Remember: DNA is replicated in the S phase, but chromosome segregation (mitosis) occurs only during the M phase.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৮) Synapsis occurs in......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis. It occurs specifically in the zygotene stage, where homologous chromosomes align precisely with the help of the synaptonemal complex, forming bivalents. In the subsequent pachytene stage, crossing over (genetic recombination) takes place between non-sister chromatids. During diplotene, the synaptonemal complex disappears, homologous chromosomes begin to separate, and chiasmata become visible. Leptotene is characterized by chromosome condensation without pairing.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Leptotene: Chromosome condensation begins.

  • Zygotene: Synapsis occurs; bivalents are formed.

  • Pachytene: Crossing over occurs.

  • Diplotene: Chiasmata become visible.

  • Diakinesis: Terminalization of chiasmata and maximal chromosome condensation.

Exam Pearl: Synapsis occurs in zygotene, whereas crossing over occurs in pachytene—a classic and frequently tested distinction.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৮৯) All are the criterias of meiotic cell division except.......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Meiosis is a specialized cell division that occurs in germ (sex) cells, producing four haploid daughter cells from one diploid parent cell. A characteristic feature of meiosis I is crossing over, which occurs during the pachytene stage of prophase I, increasing genetic diversity. During meiotic division, chromosomes are highly condensed and clearly visible under the microscope, especially from prophase I onward. Therefore, the statement "chromosomes are not visible" is incorrect and is the exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Meiosis occurs in germ cells to produce gametes.

  • Produces 4 haploid daughter cells.

  • Crossing over occurs in pachytene of prophase I.

  • Synapsis occurs in zygotene.

  • Chromosomes are condensed and visible during meiotic division.

Exam Pearl: Visible chromosomes, synapsis, and crossing over are hallmark features of meiosis; chromosomes are not invisible during meiotic division.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯০) Determination of sex of individual is possible at the time of......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The genetic sex of an individual is determined at the moment of fertilization, when the sperm carrying either an X chromosome or a Y chromosome fuses with the ovum, which always contributes an X chromosome. Fertilization by an X-bearing sperm produces an XX (female) zygote, whereas fertilization by a Y-bearing sperm produces an XY (male) zygote. Although the gonads and external genitalia differentiate later during embryonic development, the chromosomal sex is established at fertilization. Therefore, implantation, cleavage, and gastrulation occur after sex has already been determined.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ovum: Always carries an X chromosome.

  • Sperm: Carries either X or Y chromosome.

  • XX = Female, XY = Male.

  • SRY gene on the Y chromosome initiates testis development.

  • Sex is genetically determined at fertilization, while phenotypic differentiation occurs later.

Exam Pearl: The sperm determines the sex of the offspring because the ovum always contributes an X chromosome, whereas the sperm contributes either X or Y.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯১) Parasympathetic system is also called.....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system is called the craniosacral outflow because its preganglionic neurons originate from the brainstem (via cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X) and the sacral spinal cord segments S2–S4. It is responsible for "rest and digest" functions, including decreased heart rate, increased gastrointestinal motility and secretion, bronchoconstriction, and pupillary constriction. In contrast, the sympathetic nervous system arises from the T1–L2 spinal cord segments and is therefore known as the thoracolumbar outflow.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Parasympathetic outflow: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4.

  • Sympathetic outflow: T1–L2 (thoracolumbar).

  • Parasympathetic functions: Rest and digest.

  • Vagus nerve (CN X) supplies most thoracic and abdominal viscera.

  • Parasympathetic ganglia are located near or within target organs.

Exam Pearl: Parasympathetic = Craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4);

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯২) Which cranial nerves arise from pontomedullary junction?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The pontomedullary junction (pontomedullary sulcus) is the site of emergence of the abducens (CN VI), facial (CN VII), and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerves. The abducens nerve emerges near the midline, while the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves emerge more laterally at the cerebellopontine angle. In contrast, the glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and accessory (CN XI) nerves arise from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla, and the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the preolivary sulcus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pontomedullary junction: CN VI, VII, VIII.

  • Midbrain: CN III, IV.

  • Pons: CN V.

  • Medulla: CN IX, X, XI, XII.

  • CN VII and VIII emerge at the cerebellopontine angle.

Exam Pearl: The pontomedullary junction gives rise to CN VI, VII, and VIII—a classic anatomy question in MBBS and postgraduate examinations.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৩) Which one is largest cell of cerebellar cortex?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Purkinje cells are the largest neurons of the cerebellar cortex and are located in the Purkinje cell layer between the molecular and granular layers. They have extensive, highly branched dendritic trees that receive input from parallel fibers and climbing fibers. Purkinje cells are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex and are GABAergic, providing inhibitory signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei. In contrast, granule cells are the smallest and most numerous neurons in the brain, while Golgi and basket cells are inhibitory interneurons.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Purkinje cells are the largest neurons of the cerebellar cortex.

  • They are GABAergic and provide the only output from the cerebellar cortex.

  • Granule cells are the smallest and most numerous neurons in the CNS.

  • Cerebellar cortex has three layers: molecular, Purkinje, and granular.

  • Climbing fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) and parallel fibers synapse on Purkinje cells.

Exam Pearl: Purkinje cells are the largest cerebellar cortical neurons and the sole efferent neurons of the cerebellar cortex, exerting inhibitory (GABAergic) control over the deep cerebellar nuclei.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৪) Which is not a nucleus of cerebellum?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The deep cerebellar nuclei are four paired nuclei embedded within the cerebellar white matter: dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial. These nuclei receive inhibitory input from Purkinje cells and serve as the major output pathways of the cerebellum. The term "fascicular" does not refer to a cerebellar nucleus; it is associated with fasciculi (fiber tracts) in the nervous system. Therefore, fascicular is not a nucleus of the cerebellum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Deep cerebellar nuclei (lateral → medial):

    • Dentate

    • Emboliform

    • Globose

    • Fastigial

  • Mnemonic: Don't Eat Greasy Food (Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial).

  • Purkinje cells provide inhibitory (GABAergic) output to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

  • Dentate nucleus is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus.

Exam Pearl: The deep cerebellar nuclei are Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, and Fastigial (DEGF); "Fascicular" is not one of them.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৫) Visual area is situated in......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) is located in the occipital lobe, mainly along the banks of the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere. It receives visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus via the optic radiations. The surrounding visual association areas (Brodmann areas 18 and 19) process higher-order visual functions such as object recognition, color, and motion. The frontal lobe contains the motor cortex, the parietal lobe contains the primary somatosensory cortex, and the temporal lobe contains the primary auditory cortex.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Primary visual cortex: Brodmann area 17.

  • Visual association cortex: Brodmann areas 18 and 19.

  • Located along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe.

  • Receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).

  • Lesions of the primary visual cortex may cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

Exam Pearl: Vision is processed in the occipital lobe—Primary visual cortex = Brodmann area 17; Visual association cortex = Areas 18 and 19.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৬) Thalamus is a great sensory relay station for sensations except....?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The thalamus is the major sensory relay station of the brain, transmitting almost all sensory information to the cerebral cortex. It relays visual impulses through the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), auditory impulses through the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN), and gustatory (taste) sensations via the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus. Olfaction is the exception because it reaches the primary olfactory cortex directly from the olfactory bulb without an initial relay in the thalamus. Although the thalamus is involved in higher-order olfactory processing, it is not the primary relay station for smell.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thalamus relays all major sensory modalities except olfaction.

  • LGN: Vision.

  • MGN: Hearing (audition).

  • VPM nucleus: Taste (gustation) and facial sensation.

  • Olfactory pathway bypasses the thalamus initially and projects directly to the primary olfactory cortex.

Exam Pearl: The thalamus relays every sensory modality except smell (olfaction), making olfaction the classic exception in neuroanatomy.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৭) Where temperature control centre of hypothalamus lies?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
xplanation: The hypothalamus is the principal center for thermoregulation. The anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area) functions as the heat-loss center, responding to increased body temperature by promoting sweating, cutaneous vasodilation, and reduced heat production. In contrast, the posterior hypothalamus acts as the heat-conservation (heat-gain) center, initiating shivering, cutaneous vasoconstriction, and increased metabolic activity in response to cold. Therefore, when asked for the temperature control center, the most accepted examination answer is the anterior hypothalamus, as it contains the primary thermoregulatory neurons.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area): Heat-loss center.

  • Posterior hypothalamus: Heat-conservation (heat-gain) center.

  • Anterior lesion: Hyperthermia due to impaired heat dissipation.

  • Posterior lesion: Hypothermia due to impaired heat conservation.

  • Hypothalamus also regulates hunger, thirst, circadian rhythm, endocrine function, and autonomic activity.

Exam Pearl: Anterior hypothalamus = "A for Air conditioning" (heat loss); Posterior hypothalamus = heat preservation and shivering.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৮) In bell's palsy which type of lesion occurs......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), usually caused by inflammation and edema of the nerve within the facial canal. Because it is an LMN lesion, there is ipsilateral paralysis of both the upper and lower muscles of facial expression, including inability to wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile on the affected side. In contrast, an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion typically spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial muscles. Pseudobulbar palsy is a bilateral UMN disorder affecting corticobulbar tracts and is unrelated to Bell's palsy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bell's palsy = LMN lesion of CN VII.

  • Causes ipsilateral paralysis of the entire half of the face.

  • Forehead involvement distinguishes LMN from UMN facial palsy.

  • May present with hyperacusis, loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and decreased lacrimation depending on the site of the lesion.

  • Common management: Corticosteroids, with eye protection to prevent corneal injury.

Exam Pearl: Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy—both the upper and lower facial muscles on the affected side are paralyzed.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ৯৯) Which artery doesn't participate in the formation of circle of willis?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
Explanation: The Circle of Willis is an arterial anastomotic ring at the base of the brain that provides collateral cerebral circulation. It is formed by the anterior cerebral arteries, anterior communicating artery, internal carotid arteries, posterior communicating arteries, and posterior cerebral arteries. Although the middle cerebral artery (MCA) is a major terminal branch of the internal carotid artery and supplies a large portion of the cerebral hemisphere, it does not form part of the Circle of Willis. Therefore, the middle cerebral artery is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Components of the Circle of Willis:

    • Anterior cerebral arteries (2)

    • Anterior communicating artery (1)

    • Internal carotid arteries (terminal parts) (2)

    • Posterior communicating arteries (2)

    • Posterior cerebral arteries (2)

  • Middle cerebral artery is not part of the Circle of Willis.

  • Berry aneurysms commonly occur at branches of the Circle of Willis.

  • MCA stroke is the most common ischemic stroke.

Exam Pearl: The middle cerebral artery is the largest branch of the internal carotid artery but is not a component of the Circle of Willis.

Subject Final 01 Anatomy.question: ১০০) Posterior surface of manubrium sterni not related to......?
Subject Final 01 Anatomy.exp:
The posterior surface of the manubrium sterni is related to important superior mediastinal structures, including the arch of the aorta, the brachiocephalic (innominate) trunk, and the left common carotid artery, all of which arise from or are closely related to the arch of the aorta. In contrast, the right common carotid artery is not directly related to the posterior surface of the manubrium. It begins behind the right sternoclavicular joint as a terminal branch of the brachiocephalic trunk and ascends in the neck. Hence, it is the exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Posterior to the manubrium sterni lie:

    • Arch of the aorta

    • Brachiocephalic trunk

    • Left common carotid artery

    • Left brachiocephalic vein

    • Trachea

  • Right common carotid artery begins behind the right sternoclavicular joint.

  • The brachiocephalic trunk divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

Exam Pearl: The right common carotid artery is not a direct posterior relation of the manubrium because it originates at the right sternoclavicular joint from the brachiocephalic trunk.
